Fix α∈Ω. If β=gα, then normality of H gives
g(Hα)=(gHg−1)(gα)=Hβ.
(1)
Thus the transitive group action of G permutes the orbits of a group action of H, so all H-orbits have the same cardinality d. They partition the prime-sized set Ω, hence d divides ∣Ω∣. The only possibilities are d=1 and d=∣Ω∣. The first would make every element of H fix every point, contrary to the assumption that H acts nontrivially. Therefore d=∣Ω∣ and
H acts transitively on Ω​.
(2)
Now suppose H∩Gα​={1}. Define the orbit map
θ:H⟶Ω,θ(h)=hα.
(3)
It is surjective by transitivity of H. If θ(h1​)=θ(h2​), then h2−1​h1​∈H∩Gα​, so h1​=h2​; hence θ is bijective. For k∈Gα​,
θ(khk−1)=khk−1α=khα=kθ(h).
(4)
Thus θ is an equivariant map: conjugation by Gα​ on H corresponds exactly to the given action of Gα​ on Ω.

Gauss lemma for polynomials states that the product of two primitive polynomials over a unique factorization domain is primitive. In particular, a primitive polynomial in Z[X] is reducible over Q exactly when it is reducible over Z.
Eisenstein criterion says that a primitive polynomial
F(X)=an​Xn+⋯+a0​∈Z[X]
(48)
is irreducible over Q if there is a prime p such that p∤an​, p∣aj​ for every j<n, and p2∤a0​. To prove it, suppose F=GH with both factors of positive degree. After removing contents, Gauss's lemma lets us take G,H∈Z[X] primitive. Reduction modulo p gives
F=an​Xn=GH,
(49)
so both reduced factors are monomials of positive degree. Their constant terms are therefore divisible by p, making p2 divide a0​=G(0)H(0), a contradiction.
An algebraic integer is a complex number satisfying a monic polynomial in Z[X]. Let α be one and let mα​∈Q[X] be its monic minimal polynomial. The usual proof using polynomial content shows that mα​∈Z[X]. The set
Iα​={f∈Z[X]:f(α)=0}
(50)
is the kernel of the polynomial-evaluation ring homomorphism, hence an ideal. Every f∈Iα​ is divisible by mα​ in Q[X]. Because mα​ is monic, polynomial division of f by mα​ takes place in Z[X], and the remainder must vanish by minimality. Therefore
Iα​=(mα​)​,
(51)
where mα​ is monic and irreducible.
For
f(X)=X4+2X3−3X2−4X−11,
(52)
translation gives
f(X+1)=X4+6X3+9X2−15.
(53)
This is Eisenstein at p=3, so f(X+1) and therefore f(X) are irreducible over Q. Hence
Q[X]/(f) is a field​.
(54)
Irreducibility and Gauss's lemma also show that (f) is a prime ideal of Z[X], so
Z[X]/(f) is an integral domain​.
(55)
It is not a field. The class of 2 is nonzero but not a unit: reducing further modulo 2 gives a nonzero quotient
F2​[X]/(f​),
(56)
in which the image of 2 is zero, whereas a unit must remain a unit under every unital quotient map. Thus
Z[X]/(f) is not a field​.
(57)

For a continuously differentiable curve γ(t)=x(t)+iy(t) in the Poincare half-plane model, its hyperbolic length is
LH​(γ)=∫ab​y(t)x˙(t)2+y˙​(t)2​​dt​.
(69)
The hyperbolic lines are the geodesics: vertical Euclidean lines and Euclidean semicircles whose centres lie on the real axis.
The unique hyperbolic line through distinct z,w∈H can be carried by an upper-half-plane Möbius transformation to the imaginary axis. Such transformations are isometries by hypothesis, so it is enough to consider endpoints iy0​ and iy1​. Every joining curve satisfies
LH​(γ)≥∫ab​y∣y˙​∣​dt≥​logy0​y1​​​.
(70)
Equality holds for the monotone vertical parametrization
γ(t)=iy0​exp(tlogy0​y1​​),0≤t≤1.
(71)
Thus the appropriately parametrized hyperbolic-line segment [z,w] attains the infimum defining ρ(z,w).
Now let l,m have positive infimum distance. They neither intersect nor share an ideal endpoint: an intersection would give distance zero directly, while lines sharing an ideal endpoint approach one another arbitrarily closely near that endpoint. Hence they are ultraparallel. An upper-half-plane isometry puts them into the form
l={reiθ:0<θ<π},m={Reiθ:0<θ<π},0<r<R.
(72)
This is the normal form underlying the common perpendicular of ultraparallel hyperbolic lines. Put z=eu+iθ. Since
dx2+dy2=e2u(du2+dθ2),y=eusinθ,
(73)
the metric becomes
ds2=sin2θdu2+dθ2​.
(74)
Every path from l to m therefore has
LH​≥∫∣du∣≥logrR​.
(75)
Equality requires θ=π/2 and monotone u, so it is attained on the imaginary axis, which meets both semicircles orthogonally. Its intersection points ir and iR realize the distance
d=log(R/r)​.
(76)
For a nonattained example, take the vertical lines l={iy:y>0} and m={1+iy:y>0}. They share the ideal endpoint at infinity. The horizontal segment at height y has hyperbolic length 1/y, so their infimum distance is zero, but distinct points of H always have positive distance. Hence the infimum is not attained.

Equation (1) is Laplace equation for the velocity potential. It expresses incompressibility, ∇⋅u=0, together with u=∇ϕ. Equation (2) is the linearized dynamic free-surface condition: the unsteady Bernoulli equation and constant atmospheric pressure balance the potential acceleration against the gravitational restoring term gζ. Equation (3), with the printed c understood as ζ, is the kinematic free-surface condition: the surface moves with the vertical fluid velocity. Equations (4) and (5) are no-penetration boundary conditions at the rigid bottom and cylindrical sidewall, respectively.

a OurBigBook.com
A one-step or linear multistep method has order p if, when the exact sufficiently smooth solution is substituted for the numerical values, its unscaled local truncation error is O(hp+1), and this estimate is not generally O(hp+2). For a stable method this corresponds to a global error of order O(hp) on a fixed time interval.

b OurBigBook.com
Expand the exact solution about tn+1​=t. The left side is
y(t+h)−y(t)=hy′+2h2​y′′+6h3​y′′′+24h4​y(4)+O(h5).
(140)
Since f(t,y(t))=y′(t), the right side expands as
hy′+h2(1+2α+β)y′′+2h3​(1−β)y′′′+6h4​(1+2α+β)y(4)+O(h5).
(141)
The hy′ terms agree for every α,β, so the method is always consistent and is generically of order one.
The method is explicit exactly when 1+α=0. With α=−1, its h2 defect vanishes only for β=3/2, so a generic explicit member has order one; that exceptional explicit member has order two and cannot satisfy the next order condition.
For the unrestricted method to have order at least three, the h2 and h3 coefficients must agree:
1+2α+β=21​,21−β​=61​.
(142)
Solving gives
α=−127​,β=32​​.
(143)
For these values, 1+2α+β=1/2, so the right-side h4 coefficient is 1/12, different from the left-side coefficient 1/24. Hence the order is exactly three.

The first characteristic polynomial of the linear multistep method comes only from its left side:
ρ(ζ)=ζ2−ζ=ζ(ζ−1).
(144)
Its roots are zero and one; both lie in the closed unit disc, and the only unit-modulus root is simple. Thus the method satisfies the root condition for a multistep method and is zero-stable. Part (b) showed consistency for every α,β. The Dahlquist equivalence theorem states that a consistent linear multistep method is convergent exactly when it is zero-stable. Therefore
the method is convergent​
(145)
under the usual Lipschitz hypotheses on f.

The Lagrangian sufficiency theorem for a maximization problem says the following. Suppose the constraints are gi​(q)≥0 and hj​(q)=0, and define
L(q,λ,μ)=f(q)+∑i​λi​gi​(q)+∑j​μj​hj​(q),λi​≥0.
(159)
If a feasible q∗ satisfies complementary slackness λi​gi​(q∗)=0 and globally maximizes L(⋅,λ,μ), then q∗ globally maximizes f. Indeed, for every feasible q,
f(q)≤L(q,λ,μ)≤L(q∗,λ,μ)=f(q∗).
(160)
This proves the theorem. In a concave maximization problem, stationarity and the boundary optimality conditions ensure the required global maximum of the Lagrangian.
For the problem at hand, retain x,z≥0 as the domain and attach a multiplier λ to the equality:
L=x+y+2a1+z​+λ(b−x−21​y2−z).
(161)
For λ≥1, this is concave in (x,y,z) on the domain. Its separate maximizers satisfy
y=λ1​,z=max(λ2a2​−1,0),
(162)
while the x term is (1−λ)x. Thus x may be positive only when λ=1; when λ>1, its maximizing value is x=0.
If
b≥a2−21​,
(163)
take λ=1. Then y=1, z=a2−1, and feasibility fixes
x=b−a2+21​≥0.
(164)
The Lagrangian sufficiency theorem gives the maximum
(x,y,z)=(b−a2+21​,1,a2−1)​,
(165)
fmax​=b+a2+23​​.
(166)
If
21​≤b<a2−21​,
(167)
then λ>1 and x=0. The equality constraint becomes
2λ21​+λ2a2​−1=b,
(168)
so
λ2=b+1a2+1/2​.
(169)
Consequently
x=0,y=2a2+12(b+1)​​,z=2a2+12a2b−1​​.
(170)
The assumptions a≥1 and b≥1/2 ensure z≥0. At the stationary point 1+z​=ay, so the maximum value is
fmax​=(1+2a2)y=2(b+1)(2a2+1)​​.
(171)
The two formulas agree at b=a2−1/2.
